description: The Qur'an as revelation, visions in Islam, the Qur'an as miracle, and Humanist counter-arguments.
content_html:
Revelation in Islam

Revelation is fundamental to Islamic theology. Muslims believe that Allah has communicated his will to humanity through a succession of prophets and revealed books, culminating in the Qur’an as the final, complete and perfectly preserved revelation. Surah 34:46–50 addresses the prophet Muhammad directly: “I advise you only to one thing — that you stand up to Allah in pairs and alone, then reflect.” The passage makes clear that revelation comes from Allah alone, not from human invention or external inspiration. Muslims understand the Qur’an as the direct speech of Allah, transmitted through the angel Jibril to Muhammad over approximately 23 years (610–632 CE).

This understanding of the Qur’an as direct divine speech — not a book about God but God’s own words — distinguishes Islamic revelation from most Christian understandings of the Bible. For Sunni Muslims, the Qur’an is perfectly preserved and its Arabic text is the literal word of Allah; translations are always considered interpretations rather than the Qur’an itself. Shi’a Muslims share this fundamental conviction but may also attach great importance to the interpretive role of the Imams in understanding revelation. Sufi Muslims additionally emphasise the inner, experiential dimension of revelation — seeking not merely intellectual understanding of Allah’s words but transformative encounter with the divine reality they point to.

Key Fact

Surah 34:46–50 establishes that the message of Muhammad comes from Allah alone. Muslims believe the Qur’an is the direct speech of Allah transmitted through Jibril — not a human composition, which is why it carries absolute authority. The Arabic text is considered the literal word of Allah; translations are interpretations.

Visions in Islam

Visions are recognised in Islamic tradition as one of the ways in which Allah communicates. The Qur’an itself records a vision of the Virgin Mary: Surah 19:16–22 describes the angel Jibril appearing to Maryam in the form of a man, announcing the miraculous birth of Isa (Jesus). The passage presents this vision as a direct divine intervention — Jibril speaks and Maryam conceives Isa by divine command. For Muslims, this vision confirms both the reality of divine communication and the elevated status of Maryam and Isa within Islam.

Islamic tradition also includes the concept of ru’ya (true dreams) as a form of divine communication, particularly important in the Sufi tradition. The Prophet Muhammad is reported to have received early communications from Allah through true dreams. Sunni and Shi’a Muslims both recognise visions and true dreams as potentially real experiences of divine communication, though they exercise caution — not every claimed vision is accepted as genuine. The scholarly tradition requires such experiences to be consistent with the Qur’an and Sunnah.

The Qur’an as a Miracle

In Islam, the greatest miracle is not a dramatic supernatural event but the Qur’an itself. Surah 17:84–89 issues a challenge to those who doubt the divine origin of the Qur’an: “Say: if all of humanity and the jinn were to come together to produce the like of this Qur’an, they could not produce the like of it, even if they were to help one another.” This is known in Islamic theology as the Inimitability of the Qur’an (i’jaz al-Qur’an). Muslims point to the Qur’an’s literary perfection in Arabic, its internal consistency, its preservation without corruption over fourteen centuries, and its ability to transform individuals and communities as evidence that it cannot be of human origin.

Atheists and Humanists challenge Islamic claims about the Qur’an and visions on several grounds. First, they argue that beauty or complexity in a text is not evidence of divine authorship — many great works of literature are produced by human genius. Second, they point out that every religious tradition claims its own scriptures are uniquely authoritative, yet these claims are mutually contradictory — they cannot all be right, so the fact of the claim provides no proof. Third, visions (including those of Jibril appearing to Maryam and to Muhammad) may have natural psychological explanations rather than supernatural ones. Muslims respond that the inimitability challenge has stood for over 1,400 years without a convincing human response; that the consistency of the Qur’an’s themes and its preservation are themselves remarkable; and that the transformation it produces in believers’ lives is evidence of a real source beyond human invention.

Key Fact

The Inimitability of the Qur’an (i’jaz al-Qur’an) is stated in Surah 17:88: no human or group of humans could produce a text equal to the Qur’an. Muslims point to its Arabic literary perfection, 1,400-year preservation, and internal consistency as evidence of divine origin — making the Qur’an itself the primary miracle of Islam.
exam_tip_html: The key sources for this lesson are Surah 34:46–50 (revelation), Surah 19:16–22 (the vision of Maryam) and Surah 17:84–89 (the Qur’an as miracle). For the 5-mark source question, use the surah number and verse range — “In Surah 17:84–89, the Qur’an challenges all humanity and the jinn to produce a text equal to it.” For the 12-mark Discuss, develop the atheist/Humanist arguments in full and give the Muslim responses equal depth. Remember to mention Sunni, Shi’a and Sufi perspectives where relevant — this shows understanding of diversity within Islam. SPaG marks: Qur’an, revelation, inimitability, Maryam.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The Qur’an is the direct speech of Allah transmitted through Jibril — Surah 34:46–50 establishes revelation as coming from Allah alone. Sunni, Shi’a and Sufi Muslims all affirm this, with Sufis additionally emphasising transformative personal encounter.
  • Visions are recognised in Islam as divine communication — Surah 19:16–22 records Jibril appearing to Maryam. Muslims distinguish genuine visions (consistent with Qur’an and Sunnah) from false ones.
  • The primary miracle of Islam is the Qur’an itself (Surah 17:84–89) — its inimitability (i’jaz) is the standing challenge that no human could produce its equal. Atheists challenge this; Muslims point to its 1,400-year preservation and literary perfection.

practice_questions.text: Outline three Muslim beliefs about the Qur'an as revelation.
practice_questions.marks: One mark for each of three discrete points: the Qur'an is the direct speech of Allah, transmitted through the angel Jibril to Muhammad (1); it is the final and complete revelation, superseding earlier scriptures (1); its Arabic text is the literal word of Allah — translations are interpretations, not the Qur'an itself (1).

practice_questions.text: Describe the vision in Surah 19:16-22 and its significance for Muslims.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 3 marks: the angel Jibril appeared to Maryam (the Virgin Mary) in human form (1); he announced the miraculous birth of Isa (Jesus) — a child to be born without a human father, by divine command (1); this vision is significant because it confirms both the reality of divine communication through visions and the elevated status of Maryam and Isa in Islamic theology (1).

practice_questions.text: Explain two reasons why Muslims believe the Qur'an is a miracle.
practice_questions.marks: 2 marks per reason (1 for a stated point, 2 for a developed explanation). For example: Surah 17:88 issues the challenge that no human or group could produce a text equal to the Qur'an — and in 1,400 years no convincing human response to this challenge has been produced (2); the Qur'an's internal consistency, its Arabic literary perfection, and its preservation without corruption over fourteen centuries are presented as evidence that no human author could have produced it (2).

practice_questions.text: Explain two Muslim reasons for believing the Qur'an provides evidence for the existence of Allah, including a reference to a source of wisdom and authority.
practice_questions.marks: 2 marks per reason; 1 mark for a named source. Example: Surah 17:84-89 challenges all humanity to produce a text equal to the Qur'an — Muslims argue that the inimitability of the Qur'an is a standing miracle proving its divine origin (2); the Qur'an's ability to transform individuals and communities — from 7th-century Arabia to contemporary Muslims worldwide — suggests a source beyond human authorship (2); source credit for Surah 17:84-89 or Surah 34:46-50 named explicitly with surah number (1).

practice_questions.text:
'The Qur'an as a miracle is the most convincing argument that Allah exists.'
Discuss this statement.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (10-12): Both sides developed with named sources; explicit weighing; justified conclusion. Muslim case: Surah 17:88 — the inimitability challenge; 1,400-year preservation; transformation of individuals and communities. Counter: atheists argue beauty in a text is not proof of divine authorship; other traditions also claim their scriptures are uniquely authoritative; psychological explanations for visions exist. Evaluate whether the Qur'an as miracle is stronger or weaker than other arguments (design, cosmological, religious experience). Secure (7-9): Both sides present, surah named. Developing (4-6): One side dominant. Emerging (1-3): Brief, one-sided. SPaG: revelation, inimitability, Qur'an, Maryam.

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which Sunni, Shi'a and Sufi Muslims may differ in their understanding of revelation, including a reference to a source of wisdom and authority.
practice_questions.marks: 2 marks per difference; 1 mark for a named source. Example: Sunni Muslims emphasise the authority of the Qur'an and Sunnah as the complete and final revelation — Surah 34:46-50 establishes this — and the role of scholarly consensus (ijma) in interpreting it (2); Sufi Muslims seek not merely intellectual understanding of Qur'anic revelation but transformative personal encounter with Allah — dhikr (remembrance) practices aim to make the reality of Allah's presence known in direct experience (2); source credit for Surah 34:46-50 named explicitly (1).

knowledge_checks.q: What does Surah 17:88 (the inimitability challenge) say about the Qur'an?
options: The Qur'an was written by Muhammad with help from his companions
If all of humanity and the jinn came together, they could not produce a text equal to the Qur'an
The Qur'an is a translation of earlier scriptures given to Moses
Only scholars can fully understand the Qur'an
Muhammad's first revelation from Jibril in the cave of Hira
The angel Jibril appearing to Maryam and announcing the miraculous birth of Isa
Allah speaking directly to Moses from a burning bush
The Night Journey and Ascension of the Prophet

knowledge_checks.q: The Qur'an's inimitability (i'jaz al-Qur'an) is stated in Surah _____, which challenges all humanity to produce a comparable text.
Muslims believe the Qur'an is the direct speech of _____, transmitted through the angel Jibril to the Prophet Muhammad.
Match each surah to its significance for revelation, visions and miracles:
right: The message of Muhammad comes from Allah alone — not human invention
Jibril appears to Maryam and announces the birth of Isa
The Qur'an's inimitability challenge — no human could produce its equal

flashcard_questions.a: The process by which Allah communicates his will to humanity — the Qur'an is the direct, final and complete revelation.

flashcard_questions.q: What does Surah 34:46-50 establish about the source of the Qur'an?
flashcard_questions.a: That the message comes from Allah alone — not a human composition or external invention.
The Arabic name for the Virgin Mary — honoured in the Qur'an as a righteous woman chosen above all others, mother of Isa.

flashcard_questions.q: What does Surah 19:16-22 record about a vision?
flashcard_questions.a: Jibril appearing to Maryam in human form, announcing the miraculous birth of Isa by divine command.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the Inimitability of the Qur'an (i'jaz al-Qur'an)?
flashcard_questions.a: The teaching from Surah 17:88 that no human could produce a text equal to the Qur'an — it is proof of divine origin.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the Sufi approach to revelation?
flashcard_questions.a: Sufis seek not just intellectual understanding of the Qur'an but transformative personal encounter with Allah's presence.

flashcard_questions.q: How do Sunni Muslims understand the authority of the Qur'an?
flashcard_questions.a: As the direct speech of Allah, perfectly preserved — the Arabic text is authoritative; translations are interpretations only.

flashcard_questions.q: What are two pieces of evidence Muslims give for the Qur'an being a miracle?
flashcard_questions.a: Its Arabic literary perfection and its 1,400-year preservation without corruption.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the main atheist challenge to the Qur'an as a miracle?
flashcard_questions.a: Literary beauty or complexity is not proof of divine authorship — human genius can produce great texts.

flashcard_questions.q: What is a 'true dream' (ru'ya) in Islam?
flashcard_questions.a: A dream understood as a form of divine communication — the Prophet received early revelations through such dreams.

glossary_terms.definition: The process by which Allah communicates his will and guidance to humanity — in Islam, the Qur'an is the direct, final and complete revelation.
The Arabic name for the Virgin Mary, mother of Isa (Jesus), honoured in the Qur'an as a righteous woman chosen above all others.
An extraordinary event or object that points to the power and reality of Allah — in Islam the greatest miracle is the Qur'an itself.
The Qur'anic challenge (Surah 17:88) that no human being or group could produce a text equal to the Qur'an — evidence of its divine origin.
Muslims who follow the tradition of Islamic mysticism, emphasising direct personal experience of Allah's presence through devotional practices.
Muslims who follow the Sunni branch of Islam, emphasising the authority of the Qur'an, the Sunnah of the Prophet, and scholarly consensus.
Muslims who follow the Shi'a branch of Islam, emphasising the authority of the Prophet's family (Ahl al-Bayt) and the Imams.
